etymology.historical_story: The English turning verb veer is traced to French virer, meaning to turn. English additionally has a historically separate nautical verb concerning letting out rope, so identical spelling does not guarantee a single origin. Neither history establishes a Malay borrowing. Malay uses Vietnam as a complete foreign place name; its historical components are not Malay prefixes or suffixes. etymology.historical_story: J. K. Rowling invented Voldemort as a name with French associations: vol can suggest flight or theft, while mort means death. Within the story, Tom Marvolo Riddle rearranges his name into “I am Lord Voldemort,” creating a grander identity. These associations connect the name with his obsession with death; they are not Malay word formation. See [the official account](https://www.harrypotter.com/features/the-different-meanings-behind-lord-voldemorts-many-names).

etymology.historical_story: Valentine comes through English from the personal name associated with Saint Valentine; the name ultimately reflects Latin Valentinus. etymology.historical_story: Vaksin belongs to an international medical word family ultimately linked to Latin vacca, meaning cow. The connection recalls Edward Jenner's 1796 use of cowpox material to protect against smallpox. The name later extended beyond that particular disease. In Malay, the borrowed noun supports local formations such as memvaksin and pemvaksinan, connecting an international scientific term with everyday Malay grammar. etymology.historical_story: Malay borrowed vegetarian as a complete English word. Its English history is tied to nineteenth-century dietary reform: the [Vegetarian Society](https://vegsoc.org/who-we-are/history/) documents its appearance in an 1842 journal and the society's establishment in 1847. etymology.historical_story: Vertigo ultimately comes from Latin vertigo, meaning a turning round, and belongs to the word family of vertere, 'to turn'. etymology.historical_story: The international vampire word spread through Europe from Serbian vampir, with German and French helping carry it into other languages during the eighteenth century. Reports about supposed returning corpses made the term widely discussed. Its deeper origin remains debated; the immediate route by which this particular spelling entered Malay is not established here. [Historical linguistic study](https://edizionicafoscari.unive.it/media/pdf/books/978-88-97735-10-6/978-88-97735-10-6.pdf).

etymology.historical_story: Nama vitamin berkait dengan penyelidikan penyakit akibat kekurangan zat makanan. Pada tahun 1912, Casimir Funk memperkenalkan istilah vitamine, menggabungkan unsur vita, yakni kehidupan, dengan amine kerana beliau menyangka bahan tersebut tergolong dalam amina. Apabila diketahui bahawa tidak semua vitamin ialah amina, huruf e akhirnya digugurkan. Bentuk vitamin kemudian menjadi istilah sains antarabangsa. [Sejarah istilah vitamin](https://www.vitamin-society.jp/qa/).

etymology.historical_story: The international word veteran ultimately traces to Latin veteranus, associated with age and long experience, from vetus, meaning old. Malay preserves both the military meaning and the broader idea of an experienced practitioner. A veteran can therefore be a former soldier, an established sports competitor, or a seasoned performer; the surrounding words identify the intended field. [Etymology: Merriam-Webster](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/veteran).
